::: {.solutions}

**Show all your reasoning.** Total: **32 marks** · Suggested time: **45 minutes**.

This assignment tests the **sixteen facts** on the
[T1 concepts page](t01_divisors_primes.qmd). Close that page before you start — the point is recall, not
reading.

::: {.callout-important}
## What earns the marks

Every claim of the form *"this is not always true"* needs a **specific counterexample written down** — a
number, not a sentence. Every claim of the form *"this always holds"* needs a reason that covers **every**
case, which usually means splitting by residue or arguing from prime factorisations.

And before reasoning about a general $n$, **test $n=1,2,3,4$**.
:::

| Section | What it covers | Marks |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Recall** | the facts, stated back exactly | 8 |
| **B — Standard** | the arguments those facts are built into | 16 |
| **C — Stretch** | two results you derive yourself | 8 |

# Section A — Recall

## Question 1 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Complete each statement, and give the standard counterexample where one is asked for.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Every prime greater than $3$ has the form \_\_\_\_\_\_. The **converse** is false — give the
smallest counterexample. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) "$p\mid ab\Rightarrow p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$" requires $p$ to be \_\_\_\_\_\_. Give the
smallest counterexample when that word is dropped. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) "$b$ leaves remainder $r$ on division by $a$" means $b=aq+r$ with \_\_\_\_\_\_. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) A positive integer $N>1$ is composite $\Rightarrow$ it has a prime factor at most
\_\_\_\_\_\_. **[1]**
:::

:::

## Question 2 **[4]**

::: {.question}
State whether each is **true** or **false**. For each false one, give a counterexample.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $12\mid n^{2}\Rightarrow12\mid n$. **[1]**
&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) $n^{2}\equiv2\pmod 3$ is possible. **[1]**
&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) If $P(x)$ is irreducible over the integers, then $P(n)$ is prime for every integer $n$. **[1]**
&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) $\gcd(n,n+1)=1$ for every positive integer $n$. **[1]**
:::

## Question 6 **[4]**

::: {.question}
&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Explain why $2^{n}-1$ can only be prime when $n$ is prime. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Show that the converse fails, by finding a prime $n<15$ for which $2^{n}-1$ is
**composite**. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) $341=11\times31$ satisfies $2^{340}\equiv1\pmod{341}$. What does this tell you about the
usefulness of Fermat's little theorem as a **primality test**? **[1]**

# Section C — Stretch

## Question 7 **[4]**

::: {.question}
&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Prove that $n^{3}-n$ is divisible by $6$ for every integer $n$. **[3]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) A student writes: *"$n^{3}-n=n(n^{2}-1)$, which factorises, so $n^{3}-n$ is never prime."*
Is the conclusion true? Is the **argument** sound? **[1]**

## Before you hand this in

1. Every **false** statement should have a **number** beside it, not a sentence.
2. Where you argued "for every $n$", check you covered **every residue**, not a few examples.
3. Check $n=1$ everywhere. In this topic it is the case that breaks proofs.
:::
